Learning to Compute Is Not Learning to Retain
or Reuse in Looped Transformers

Peilong Zhou   Hongtao Zhang   Yulong Huang Affiliation: SKLP, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: School of Advanced Interdisciplinary Sciences Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)*Equal contribution.†Corresponding author. Email: wangying2009@ict.ac.cn    Cangyuan Li   Mingyu Chen   Ying Wang Affiliation: SKLP, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
Abstract

Looped transformers compute by applying one block repeatedly, so they can run for more loops than they were trained with. Recurrent reasoners are known to overthink: iterating past the trained depth can turn a correct answer into a wrong one. Such a late error can reflect failed computation, loss of retention, or a state that later computation cannot reuse. We separate these cases in in-context Mealy-machine execution, where a simulator supplies intermediate targets and exact counterfactuals for hidden-state interventions. Models trained to answer at loop 32 are fully correct there but keep only 22% of these answers at loop 64. Retention depends on what training asks for: supervising one randomly chosen position per example, instead of always the last, keeps 99.8%, and randomizing the number of training loops also helps; truncating gradients, as in progressive training against overthinking, does not. The computation itself is exact: position kk is computed at loop kk, and swapping its loop-kk hidden vector for the one from another input redirects every later position to that input’s exact continuation (237/237 pairs in each of ten models). Retention, however, is not reuse. Even in models that keep nearly all answers, holding each position kk fixed from loop kk drops accuracy to 4–6%, whereas holding it from loop k+4k+4 is harmless. A released recurrent maze network trained to avoid overthinking behaves the same way. Learning to compute is thus not learning to retain, and avoiding overthinking does not make a state reusable when its answer first appears.

1 Introduction

Looped transformers turn recurrent depth into a computation budget: one block is applied repeatedly, so a model can run for more loops than it was trained with (Dehghani et al., 2019; Giannou et al., 2023; Geiping et al., 2025). Whether those extra loops help depends on what happens to an answer after it has been computed.

Empirically, running past the trained depth can hurt. Recurrent networks trained on small instances can solve larger ones by iterating longer (Schwarzschild et al., 2021), but further iteration can also turn a correct answer into a wrong one. Bansal et al. (2022) call this failure overthinking and prevent it with input recall and progressive training, which applies the loss at a random depth and blocks gradients to the loops before a random starting point. Later work relates extra computation to path independence and shows that training and stopping objectives change the learned trajectory (Anil et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2026; Kuo et al., 2026; Popescu et al., 2026); analysis of recurrent language models separates whether content is readable from whether it is transported and can be steered (Wang and Reid, 2026). Much of this evidence tracks accuracy or readouts across loops. An overthinking curve, however, can mean three different things: the answer was never computed, it was computed but not retained, or the state that carries it cannot be reused by later computation. Telling these apart requires knowing what a correct alternative execution would be. We therefore ask: when a looped model learns to compute an answer, what does it learn about retaining that answer and reusing its internal state?

In-context execution of Mealy machines makes these distinctions measurable (Figure 1). Each example gives a transition table and an input sequence of length HH. A simulator supplies the correct state and output at every position, including after any counterfactual change, so an intervention can be scored against a unique correct continuation rather than by whether the output changed. We apply one shared transformer block for RR loops and train only on the readout after the last loop, the exit; the main models use R=HR=H, one loop per input symbol, and compare objectives that differ only in which answers must be correct at that exit: the last position (final-only), every position (all-prefix), or one uniformly sampled position per example (sampled-prefix). Endpoint accuracy requires both the state and the output at the last position to be correct. In the models we analyze, position kk first becomes correct at or near loop kk; we call the diagonal r=kr=k the frontier. Because the loop at which each answer first appears is known, a state can be tested at exactly that moment. We intervene on the recurrent trajectory in three ways: replacing a hidden vector in a base run with the corresponding vector of a source run on a different input prefix (Geiger et al., 2024), resetting a position to its own earlier vector, and freezing each position at a chosen loop. At the frontier, one position’s hidden vector suffices to drive the rest of the execution, so the same unit lets us compare what a state makes readable with what it lets later computation do.

The three properties come apart. In the order of the paper, we find:

  • •

    Retention is set by what training requires (Section 3). On shared length-32 test inputs, final-only models are 100% correct at the trained exit but 22.3% at loop 64 (Figure 2). all-prefix gives 94.3%, and sampled-prefix gives 99.8% with the same single supervised position per example as final-only. At a matched expected budget, drawing the exit as R=H+UR=H+U with UU uniform on {0,…,8}\{0,\ldots,8\}, instead of fixing R=H+4R=H+4, raises loop-64 accuracy from 30.0% to 85.6%. Truncated gradients do not help: our adaptation of progressive training learns length 32 in one of three seeds, whereas a matched random exit control with identical exits and full gradients learns it in all three and keeps 97.9% at loop 64.

  • •

    Computation is exact, but its answers are transient (Section 4). Replacing one hidden vector at the frontier redirects every later frontier readout to the exact counterfactual execution in all 237 pairs whose counterfactual differs, in each of ten final-only models (Figure 3). These answers fade soon after they are computed, in swapped and unmodified runs alike.

  • •

    Answers become readable before their states become reusable (Section 5). Freezing each position kk from the loop at which its answer first becomes readable, as per-position halting would and with no other run or label involved, reduces endpoint accuracy from 100% to 4.1% under sampled-prefix and to 6.3% under matched random exit, two objectives that retain answers well (Figure 4). Freezing two to four loops later restores it. A released recurrent maze network that never loses a solved maze solves none of 32 mazes when each pixel is frozen at its answer’s arrival, and all of them when frozen four iterations later.

These interventions separate the three properties; they do not identify a microscopic cause of ordinary decline or give a general repair. The main evidence comes from one synthetic task family and one architecture, with a limited external check (Section 7).

2 A controlled setting for computation and retention

Task and model.

A deterministic Mealy machine has a finite state set QQ, input alphabet Σ\Sigma, output alphabet Γ\Gamma, initial state q0q_{0}, transition function δ:Q×Σ→Q\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q, and output function λ:Q×Σ→Γ\lambda:Q\times\Sigma\to\Gamma. Reading a sequence of input symbols, which we call actions, a1,…,aH∈Σa_{1},\ldots,a_{H}\in\Sigma (HH is the horizon), it computes

qk=δ(qk−1,ak),yk=λ(qk−1,ak),k=1,…,H,q_{k}=\delta(q_{k-1},a_{k}),\qquad y_{k}=\lambda(q_{k-1},a_{k}),\qquad k=1,\ldots,H, (1)

so qkq_{k} is the state after action kk and yky_{k} the output emitted on that transition. In Figure 1a, from q0=Aq_{0}=A the action a1=0a_{1}=0 follows the edge 0/10/1, giving q1=Bq_{1}=B and y1=1y_{1}=1. An example xx lists q0q_{0}, one token per table entry (q,a)↦(δ⁡(q,a),λ⁡(q,a))(q,a)\mapsto(\delta(q,a),\lambda(q,a)), and the HH actions. At the token of action kk the model predicts qkq_{k} and yky_{k}; these are targets, never inputs. The generator samples reachable, behaviorally minimal machines with 4, 6, or 8 states, 2 or 4 input symbols, and 2 output symbols; randomized symbol names and row order discourage fixed-label shortcuts but do not establish structural disjointness of sampled machines (Appendix A).

The model repeats a two-layer transformer block with width 128, four attention heads, and feed-forward width 512. With input embeddings E⁡(x)E(x), it computes

X0=0,Xr=Bθ​(Xr−1+E⁡(x)).X^{0}=0,\qquad X^{r}=B_{\theta}\bigl(X^{r-1}+E(x)\bigr). (2)

Here rr indexes loops and XrX^{r} collects the hidden vectors of all tokens after loop rr; training reads out after loop RR, the exit. The block’s two layers have different parameters; the entire block is shared across loops (Figure 1b; details in Figure A1). There are no positional or loop-depth embeddings; the causal attention mask provides the architectural signal of action order.

The prefix (initial-state token and transition table) attends within itself, and action position kk attends to this prefix and actions 1:k1{:}k. Let hkrh_{k}^{r} denote its post-block hidden vector. Shared state and output heads are trained jointly with the model and read LN⁡(hkr)\operatorname{LN}(h_{k}^{r}) after each loop. Hidden-vector interventions replace hkrh_{k}^{r} before this final normalization and affect subsequent loops.

Training objectives.

Our main comparison fixes the training exit R=HR=H, architecture, curriculum, optimizer, and training duration, and changes the supervised positions at the exit. Each batch shares one horizon HH. With ℓi,kR\ell_{i,k}^{R} the sum of state and output cross-entropies for example ii, the batch objective is

ℒS=1∑i|Si|​∑i∑k∈Siℓi,kR,Si={{H},final-only,{1,…,H},all-prefix,{Ki},Ki∼U⁡{1,…,H},sampled-prefix.\mathcal{L}_{S}=\frac{1}{\sum_{i}|S_{i}|}\sum_{i}\sum_{k\in S_{i}}\ell_{i,k}^{R},\qquad S_{i}=\begin{cases}\{H\},&\textsc{final-only},\\ \{1,\ldots,H\},&\textsc{all-prefix},\\ \{K_{i}\},\ K_{i}\sim U\{1,\ldots,H\},&\textsc{sampled-prefix}.\end{cases} (3)

Relative to final-only, all-prefix broadens position coverage and increases the number of supervised state–output pairs per example from one to HH. sampled-prefix separates coverage from dense per-example supervision by selecting one position independently and uniformly per example. At fixed parameters and batch, its expected loss equals the mean all-prefix loss. All three objectives apply these losses only at the exit, not at every loop (Figure 1c), and average over selected positions rather than multiplying the loss by HH.

The main training comparisons use 132,000 AdamW steps, batch size 256, and the same 35-stage curriculum reaching H=32H=32. After the initial H=1H=1 stage, each stage draws its maximum horizon with probability .5 and otherwise a shorter horizon uniformly from 1 to one below that maximum. Under final-only, every horizon H≤32H\leq 32 therefore receives endpoint supervision at loop HH as the curriculum progresses. Because future actions cannot affect earlier positions, a length-kk input and any extension of it have identical computations at positions 1:k1{:}k when the machine presentation is unchanged. Shorter-horizon training thus directly constrains position kk at loop kk even when that prefix appears in a longer input. all-prefix and sampled-prefix additionally supervise that position at exits H>kH>k, requiring its answer to be readable H−kH-k loops beyond the diagonal r=kr=k. The relation of this diagonal to the measured first-correct frontier is evaluated in Section 3.

Section 3 also varies the exit distribution (Slack-4 versus Jitter-8) and tests gradient truncation by comparing progressive training with matched random exit at matched supervised exits.

Evaluation cohorts.

The common cohort compares final-only, all-prefix, sampled-prefix, progressive, and matched random exit on model seeds 9–11 and one shared evaluation stream; the existing final-only/all-prefix checkpoints are re-evaluated. The original cohort uses seeds 9–14 for the historical training comparisons, including Slack-4/Jitter-8, and supplies six pairs of final-only/all-prefix models for the position-16 interventions (Section 5; Appendices B.6 and C). Its behavioral evaluations use a separate stream. The position-8 transport audit in Section 4 uses ten final-only models, seeds 9–18. Overlapping checkpoints are not independent model replications. Additional freezing, larger-model, and maze cohorts are specified with their experiments in Section 5 and the appendices. No seed is selected for intervention success; Appendices A and B.1 give the seeds, streams, and pairing protocols.

Readouts and scoring.

For one model and NN evaluation examples of length HH, endpoint accuracy at readout loop rr is the fraction for which both predictions at the last action are correct:

A(H,r)=1N∑i=1N[q^i,Hr=qi,H∧y^i,Hr=yi,H].A(H,r)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{q}_{i,H}^{r}=q_{i,H}\;\land\;\hat{y}_{i,H}^{r}=y_{i,H}\right]. (4)

Whole-trajectory exactness requires both predictions at all HH positions of an example to be correct at the same loop rr, and reports the fraction of examples satisfying this conjunction. The main endpoint and trajectory evaluations use 512 traces per model and length: 16 machines with 32 traces each. Scores are computed within each model and then averaged across models with equal weight (Appendix A).

On a clean loop–position grid, τ⁡(k)\tau(k) is the first evaluated loop at which both marginal state and output accuracies at position kk reach .99, for the specified model, horizon, and evaluation set. This population criterion differs from the example-level conjunctions above. We reserve τ⁡(k)\tau(k) for this measured quantity and write s⁡(k)s(k) for a specified readout or capture schedule. The matched-frontier audit in Section 4 uses the diagonal schedule s⁡(k)=ks(k)=k; a common-exit readout uses s⁡(k)=rs(k)=r for all positions. Fixed freezing schedules and their agreement with the clean frontier are assessed separately in Section 5. Section 4 introduces source–base pairs, their counterfactual targets, and the corresponding suffix-exactness scores.

3 Training to retain changes inference-budget robustness

A correct endpoint need not survive more loops.

Figure 2a,b evaluates the common cohort, holding each input and checkpoint fixed across loops. final-only endpoint joint accuracy falls from 100% at loop 32 to 60.81% at loop 33 and 22.33% at loop 64. Whole-trajectory exactness is 0% at both loops 32 and 64. These are losses on solved inputs of unchanged length. Original-cohort results remain separate (Appendix B.2).

One supervised position per example is enough for strong retention.

At the same training exit R=HR=H, all-prefix raises loop-64 endpoint accuracy to 94.27% on the common stream, but supplies more supervised positions. sampled-prefix controls this difference: each example contributes one uniformly chosen position’s state and output losses. All three models attain 100% endpoint and whole-trajectory accuracy at loop 32. At loops 64 and 96, endpoint means are 99.80% and 96.61%, and whole-trajectory means are 96.03% and 74.09%. The corresponding all-prefix trajectory means are 74.28% and 67.45%. Dense per-example supervision is therefore not necessary for the observed retention gain. This three-seed result does not establish that sampling is generally superior to all-prefix, nor remove the need for intermediate labels.

For both baselines trained at R=HR=H, the original readability grids give a first-correct frontier τ⁡(k)=k\tau(k)=k (Appendix B.4); Section 4 tests its causal role.

Varying the exit helps at matched expected loop budgets.

The original-cohort comparison in Figure 2c retains final-only supervision and compares Slack-4, R=H+4R=H+4, with Jitter-8, R=H+U​{0,…,8}R=H+U\{0,\ldots,8\}. Both have conditional mean H+4H+4; cumulative batched block applications differ by only 0.062%. At H32/loop64, endpoint means are 30.01% and 85.55%, with Jitter-8 higher in every pair; at loop96 they are 26.79% and 79.79%. Both readouts exceed Jitter-8’s H32 training support of 32–40. The effect has tradeoffs: at the common loop36, Slack-4 gives 93.98% versus 87.27%, and some seeds do not fully learn the training length range. Appendix B.3 reports all seeds and work accounting.

Truncated gradients do not help retention.

Bansal et al. (2022) prevent overthinking with progressive training, which changes two things at once: the loss is applied at a random depth, and gradients do not reach the loops before a random starting point. We adapt it to this architecture and separate the two with a matched control. At each update, both progressive and matched random exit add to a full branch ending at m=H+8m=H+8 a second branch with a random exit n+k≥Hn+k\geq H. progressive detaches this branch after its first nn loops; matched random exit back-propagates through all n+kn+k. Examples, exits, loss weights, and updates are identical, so only the gradient path, and with it the backward work, differs (Appendix B.1).

In this recipe truncation impedes learning. Two of three progressive models never exceed 60% H32 endpoint accuracy, so their low late scores are not forgetting; the third reaches 100% at loops 40–48 and falls to 26.6% by loop 96. All three matched random exit models reach 100% at loop 32 and keep 97.9% at loop 64 (Figure 2d). Like Jitter-8, this random-exit objective keeps endpoint answers well past its training exits. Its losses, like those of final-only, use only the last position, and it keeps far fewer complete trajectories: 29.6% are exact at loop 64, against 96.0% under sampled-prefix. This is an FSM adaptation, not a reproduction of the original architecture or a ranking of progressive methods.

Retention is a distinct, finite-window property.

Supervision support does not fully explain learning or retention, and H32 retention does not guarantee improved length extrapolation. On the common H64/loop96 evaluation, sampled-prefix has 82.68% endpoint accuracy versus 93.03% for matched random exit. The original length comparison also has mixed outcomes (Appendix B.5).

4 Computation is exact, but its answers are transient

Section 3 found that each position’s answer first becomes readable at loop kk, even in final-only models that get almost no complete trajectory right at the trained exit. Readable does not mean used: a readout can decode information that the computation ignores. We therefore test whether the frontier state is what the rest of the execution runs on. If it is, replacing it with another input’s state should make the run follow that input’s execution exactly, and a simulator tells us what that execution is.

Swapping one state between two inputs.

We pair two inputs that share the machine, symbol assignment, and transition-table presentation, and differ only in their actions up to position cc; their states qcSq_{c}^{S} and qcBq_{c}^{B} at cc differ (Figure 3a). Following interchange interventions (Geiger et al., 2024), we copy the full 128-dimensional hidden vector of the source run at position cc and loop rr into the base run,

hcr←hc,Sr,h_{c}^{r}\leftarrow h_{c,S}^{r}, (5)

leave every other base position unchanged, and let the trained model continue. No symbolic state or answer enters the network. Because the remaining actions are shared, a base run that now carries the source’s state should continue exactly as the source run does. Running Equation 1 from qcSq_{c}^{S} on these actions gives this counterfactual target q~k\tilde{q}_{k} for every k>ck>c (Geiger et al., 2021). A pair is suffix-exact under a readout schedule s⁡(k)s(k) when every state and output after cc matches the target. We score only eligible pairs, whose counterfactual and factual suffixes differ, so that a run ignoring the swap cannot succeed (Appendix A).

One swapped state drives the rest of the execution.

In ten final-only models with H=32H=32, we swap at position 8 and loop 8, the loop at which position 8’s answer first becomes correct in every model (τ⁡(8)=8\tau(8)=8; Appendix A). Of 256 pairs, 237 are eligible. In every model, all 237 follow the source exactly: every state and output at positions 9 to 32, each read at loop kk (Figure 3c). One vector thus steers 24 further steps of exact symbolic execution. Copying a vector back into its own run changes no prediction, and patch scans place the damaging site on the same frontier (Appendix A). The swap shows that this state suffices to drive the computation; it does not show that the state is a unique symbolic code.

The answers do not stay.

In both the swapped and the clean run, agreement is highest on the diagonal and fades above it (Figure 3b,c): an answer is readable at the loop that computes it, and answers computed early have faded by loop 32. The near-zero whole-trajectory exactness of final-only models at the trained exit (Section 3) is therefore not a failure to compute: the intermediate answers are computed exactly and then not kept.

5 Answers become readable before their states become reusable

Halting treats a solved position as finished.

Section 3 showed that training can keep an answer readable long after it is computed, and Section 4 that a single frontier state drives the computation that follows. A position whose answer has appeared and stays readable therefore looks finished, and adaptive computation treats it that way. The Universal Transformer halts positions individually and copies a halted position’s state unchanged to every later step (Dehghani et al., 2019). Huginn stops iterating on a token once successive steps give nearly the same output distribution, and later tokens attend to its last computed key–value state (Geiping et al., 2025). Bansal et al. (2022) describe their networks, trained to avoid overthinking, as holding on to the representation of a solution once it is reached. These methods differ in when a position counts as finished. We test the earliest point, the loop at which its answer first becomes readable. Our setting makes that loop known: position kk first becomes correct at loop kk, and every position has an exact target.

Freezing applies this halting at the first readable loop.

For each position kk, we capture its hidden vector at loop kk and write it back after every later block, as copying a halted state would. All other positions update normally, frozen positions stay visible to attention, and no other run or label is involved (Figure 4a). As a control, readout caching stores each position’s loop-kk prediction outside the model and leaves every hidden state untouched; the two differ only in whether the answer or its state is kept. We call a state reusable if freezing it in this way leaves the later positions correct. We freeze six final-only, three all-prefix, and three larger final-only models (d=512d=512 and four layers per block, about 32 times the block parameters), and the three sampled-prefix and three matched random exit models of Section 3.

The answers are correct, but their states cannot yet be frozen.

In the twelve models of Figure 4b, caching keeps all 32 answers correct, so every answer is correct when it is captured. Freezing the states instead leaves at most 2% of examples fully correct. Good retention does not prevent this. sampled-prefix keeps 99.8% of its endpoint answers at loop 64 (Section 3) and its cached answers are all correct, yet freezing drops its endpoint accuracy from 100% to 4.1%. all-prefix models, which keep every position readable at the exit, and matched random exit models collapse in the same way (Appendix D). The answers stay readable; their states cannot yet stop changing.

Frozen states fail as inputs to later computation.

The errors start just downstream of the frozen states (Figure 4c). Positions 1 and 2 stay correct in every model, and position 3 is the first to fail. At loop 3 it reads the loop-2 vectors of positions 1 to 3, which differ from the clean run in one place only: position 1 has missed its loop-2 update, which came after its answer was already readable. That one missing update lowers the accuracy of position 3 to 68% in the final-only models, and errors then compound along the sequence. Freezing only positions 1–8 leaves positions 9–32 free to update, yet in the final-only models the endpoint is still correct on at most 11.9% of examples (Appendix D). A frozen state still yields its own answer, as positions 1 and 2 show, but it no longer works as input: later positions need the updates that upstream states receive after their answers appear.

A state becomes reusable two to four loops after its answer.

Delaying the capture by dd loops shows when a state can be frozen (Figure 4d). With a two-loop delay, sampled-prefix recovers to 99.8% endpoint accuracy; matched random exit needs four loops to reach the same level (Appendix D.3). An answer is readable at loop kk, but the state that carries it becomes reusable only a few loops later, and how many loops depends on the model.

The maze network trained against overthinking behaves the same way.

We apply the same test to the released maze network of Bansal et al. (2022), the model described above as holding on to its solution. Trained with 30 iterations, it solves all 32 test mazes of size 9×99\times 9 at every iteration from 25 to 120. Since mazes have no per-position frontier, we freeze each pixel at its answer’s arrival, the last iteration at which its clean prediction changes. No maze is then solved; freezing two or four iterations later solves 28 and 32, and caching the answers solves all 32 (Appendix D; one checkpoint, 32 mazes per size). The network does hold on to its solution, but only a few iterations after each answer arrives.

What freezing shows.

An answer readable at loop kk is thus not yet carried by a reusable state, even in models that retain answers almost perfectly; the state becomes reusable two to four loops later. Retention and reuse are different properties. For per-position halting in such models, stopping a position when its answer first becomes readable is too early: its state must keep updating for a few loops, or only its answer should be kept. The experiments do not show that information is lost, since cached answers stay correct, and they do not identify a mechanism. The model has no positional or loop embeddings, so the evolving state may also carry timing or order information that later positions use to find their predecessors, and freezing would hold that information as well. Our tests do not separate these possibilities; under either, a state cannot be frozen when its answer first appears. A source vector transplanted from another run shows the same dependence on timing (Appendix C).

6 Related work

Extra iterations in recurrent reasoners.

Recurrent networks trained on small instances can solve larger ones by iterating longer (Schwarzschild et al., 2021). Bansal et al. (2022) show that excessive iteration can degrade answers (“overthinking”), and prevent this with input recall and progressive training from detached intermediate states. They also test recovery after feature-map interventions and track feature convergence. We adapt their progressive loss in Section 3 and freeze their released maze network in Section 5. Anil et al. (2022) relate additional computation to path independence: convergence to the same steady state regardless of initialization. We do not claim novelty for overthinking, variable exits, or mid-computation substitution. What is new is the measurement: exact symbolic targets for every position, loop, and counterfactual, which let us test a state at the loop where its answer first appears.

These works assess stability through outputs, feature maps, or final convergence; we ask whether a state can be held from the moment its clean readout becomes correct. This is a position-level counterpart to path independence, not a test of it: we do not vary initialization.

Recurrent computation and training requirements.

Universal and looped transformers connect shared parameters to adaptive computation, programmable execution, and length generalization (Dehghani et al., 2019; Giannou et al., 2023; Fan et al., 2025); recurrent-depth language models extend this motivation to latent test-time compute (Geiping et al., 2025). Zhang et al. (2026) study budget-dependent frontiers, causal damage cones, and frontier-state transplants. We build on these observations rather than claiming novelty for frontiers or transport. A first-correct frontier differs from a convergence time that requires an answer to remain correct.

Stochastic stopping can stabilize budget-dependent behavior without better extrapolation (Kuo et al., 2026); adaptive-depth studies distinguish trajectory formation from readout selection (Popescu et al., 2026). Our comparisons instead change supervised positions at a fixed exit, or exit variability at matched expected loops; sampling one position estimates the all-position loss rather than introducing a new loss principle.

Readable and causally usable representations.

Wang and Reid (2026) distinguish readout, transport, and steering across recurrent depth in Ouro and Huginn, and associate verbalizing injected content with per-iteration supervision. Our all-prefix loss applies only at the exit; we add paired training comparisons, exact symbolic targets, and local downstream restoration that separates downstream state from execution phase.

State-tracking studies identify alternative transformer algorithms and effects of intermediate objectives (Liu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), and interchange interventions test such algorithmic hypotheses (Geiger et al., 2021; Geiger et al., 2024). Our full-vector intervention establishes sufficiency in a specified machine context, not a unique minimal encoding or complete algorithm identification.

7 Discussion and limitations

Computing an answer, retaining its readout, and reusing its representation are different properties, and each needs its own test: correctness at one exit does not test retention, and retained predictions do not test whether a hidden state can be held or reused for continuation. Supervised positions, exit distributions, and gradient propagation all change retention, and poor late accuracy can conceal a coherent earlier counterfactual computation. Retained answers need not reside in reusable states: freezing a position when its answer first becomes readable disrupts later computation, including under sampled-position training, and the state becomes reusable only a few loops later; a transplanted source likewise needs the downstream position reset before it takes effect. We have not tested downstream resets on the new training controls or stochastic-budget models, so their retention gains do not establish the same downstream mechanism.

These full-vector, post-block interventions do not identify a unique encoding, microscopic cause of forgetting, or general repair; they can change nonsymbolic features or restart computation, and downstream recovery concerns one step at one site and age. The scope is one synthetic execution family and one principal architecture, plus a limited external maze check. Original training comparisons use six paired seeds; new controls use three. Re-evaluating overlapping checkpoints is not independent model replication. Sampled supervision still needs intermediate labels. Budget controls match expected loops, and progressive controls match forward work but differ in backward work; neither matches measured total FLOPs. Finite-window retention does not establish hidden-state convergence or uniform length extrapolation.

AI use statement

The core idea of this work is the authors’ own. Generative AI tools assisted with code implementation, experiment and control iteration, literature search, translation, manuscript editing, and figure code. The authors verified the analyses, citations, and final artifacts and take full responsibility for the work.

Ethics statement

Machines and traces are procedurally generated; the work uses no personal or human-subject data. The objectives studied here do not ensure the reliability of deployed systems.

Reproducibility statement

Appendix A specifies machine generation, the network, optimization, curriculum, and scoring. Appendices B–E give every training and intervention protocol with per-seed results, and Appendix B.8 records the checkpoints, evaluation streams, pair identities, and hashes behind the principal quantities.
