Appendix A Experimental methods and scoring

A.1 Machine generation and input encoding

At each stage, the data generator samples the state count and input-alphabet size independently and uniformly from the active lists in Table A1; the output alphabet has two symbols. Generation fixes an internal initial state S0S_{0} and first makes every state reachable. In a random order of the other states, each is attached through a uniformly sampled unused state–input cell of an already reachable state. Remaining transition destinations are sampled uniformly from QQ, and each cell’s output is sampled uniformly from Γ\Gamma. Candidates are resampled until behaviorally minimal and covering both output symbols. These construction and acceptance rules make the accepted transition-table entries dependent.

Each sampled machine contributes up to 32 action traces, all starting at S0S_{0}, with actions drawn independently and uniformly from its input alphabet. A training batch contains 256 examples of the same sampled horizon. The online stream, including machine generation, action traces, and presentation randomization, is reproducible from its generator state.

The initial state is one token. Every transition is represented by one factorized token containing its source state, input symbol, destination state, and output symbol. Action tokens follow the table and contain only their input symbol. Token embeddings sum a kind embedding and the embeddings of the present symbolic fields. The global namespaces contain 16 state IDs, 8 input IDs, and 4 output IDs, although an individual machine uses only 4/6/8 states, 2/4 inputs, and 2 outputs. Each presentation assigns local symbols to randomly selected namespace IDs and shuffles the transition rows. Training does not force traces from one machine to share the same presentation; source–base pairs explicitly share a presentation to control that variable.

The attention mask lets initial-state and table tokens attend within the prefix, and action kk attend to the prefix and actions up to and including kk. It blocks all access to future actions. Padded positions are masked and zeroed through the computation. A causal action prefix therefore has the same unmodified computation when followed by additional actions of the same presented machine. This structural property helps explain why endpoint training at shorter lengths constrains earlier positions in longer examples; it does not prove a particular internal algorithm.

Training uses data seed 20260901. The original six-seed budget comparisons use evaluation seed 20260909; the five-condition, three-seed comparison uses 20260923, with the old baselines re-evaluated on that same stream. Both use four batches of 128 examples per model and length: 16 sampled machines with 32 traces each, not 512 independent machines. The new six-model freeze follow-up uses stream 20260924. Actual generator seeds add 1009​H1009H to the specified stream. The original training logs use evaluation seed 20260902. These are separate evaluation streams. We do not combine their metrics as if they came from one paired sample set. Randomized presentations and independently drawn evaluation streams do not guarantee that every machine graph is structurally absent from training.

A.2 Network, optimization, and curriculum

The shared block contains two pre-normalized transformer layers, each with four attention heads, width 128, a width-512 feed-forward network, and residual connections. Dropout is zero. The recurrence begins with a zero hidden matrix and adds the same input embedding before every block application. There is no learned recurrent gate, loop embedding, positional embedding, or enabled layer scaling. State and output linear heads follow a shared final layer normalization. The heads have 16 and 4 classes, respectively. All reported hidden-vector replacements occur after the shared block and before this final normalization, exactly as in Equation 5.

Figure A1 summarizes the input sequence, one layer, the attention mask, and the two per-loop scores.

AdamW uses initial learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} with cosine decay to zero, weight decay .01, gradient norm clipping at 1, and batch size 256. Both task losses have weight 1 and use mean cross-entropy over the selected valid positions. Training runs for the fixed 132,000-step curriculum in Table A1; stage checks are audits, not a rule for selecting a checkpoint or stopping a failing seed. Checkpoints are saved at fixed steps, and all main comparisons use step 132,000.

A.3 Readouts, thresholds, and exactness

Let Qi,krQ_{i,k}^{r} and Yi,krY_{i,k}^{r} be indicators of correct state and output for sample ii, position kk, and loop rr. The endpoint curve reports N−1​∑iQi,Hr​Yi,HrN^{-1}\sum_{i}Q_{i,H}^{r}Y_{i,H}^{r}. The grid criterion instead requires both N−1​∑iQi,kr≥.99N^{-1}\sum_{i}Q_{i,k}^{r}\geq.99 and N−1​∑iYi,kr≥.99N^{-1}\sum_{i}Y_{i,k}^{r}\geq.99. Passing this criterion is not the same as a per-sample guarantee that every state and output is correct. The first loop passing it on the clean grid defines τ⁡(k)\tau(k) for that model, horizon, and evaluation set. This measured quantity is distinct from a prescribed readout or capture schedule s⁡(k)s(k). Hold includes consecutive passing loops from τ⁡(k)\tau(k), including the first. If the measured window ends while the criterion still holds, the observed hold is a right-censored lower bound.

For the whole-trajectory metric in Figure 2, an example is trajectory-exact at readout loop rr when every one of its HH state–output pairs is correct at that same readout:

Eir=∏k=1HQi,kr​Yi,kr,TrajExact⁡(r)=N−1​∑iEir.E_{i}^{r}=\prod_{k=1}^{H}Q_{i,k}^{r}Y_{i,k}^{r},\qquad\operatorname{TrajExact}(r)=N^{-1}\sum_{i}E_{i}^{r}.

This example-level conjunction is stricter than either the endpoint event or the grid’s two marginal population thresholds.

For a target sequence (q¯i,k,y¯i,k)(\bar{q}_{i,k},\bar{y}_{i,k}) and readout schedule s⁡(k)s(k), suffix exactness on an eligible set ℰ\mathcal{E} is

Exactℰ(s)=1|ℰ|∑i∈ℰ∏k=c+1H𝟏[q^i,ks⁡(k)=q¯i,k]𝟏[y^i,ks⁡(k)=y¯i,k].\operatorname{Exact}_{\mathcal{E}}(s)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}}\prod_{k=c+1}^{H}\mathbf{1}[\hat{q}_{i,k}^{s(k)}=\bar{q}_{i,k}]\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{i,k}^{s(k)}=\bar{y}_{i,k}]. (6)

The ordinary target is the base run’s factual trajectory. The source target is the simulated counterfactual. Changing this target changes the estimand; changing s⁡(k)s(k) changes when it is observed. A wrong prediction that differs from both trajectories is not successful transport.

A.4 Position-8 transport audit

The position-8 audit uses ten serial final-only models, seeds 9–18, with H=32H=32 and a single replacement at loop 8. On a separate clean grid (evaluation stream 20260903, 512 examples per model), all ten models have τ⁡(k)=k\tau(k)=k at every position k=1,…,32k=1,\ldots,32, with state and output accuracy 1.000 on the diagonal. The same 256 different-state pairs are reused across seeds. A pair is eligible for suffix scoring if at least one state or output in positions 9–32 differs between its factual and source targets; there are 237 such pairs. Conditional exactness uses that denominator, not 256 or ten times 237 independent task samples. The matched-frontier schedule is s⁡(k)=ks(k)=k and the common-exit schedule is s⁡(k)=32s(k)=32. Eligibility requires a difference somewhere in the suffix, not at every suffix position. Factual and counterfactual states may later merge. Complete suffix agreement consequently does not establish that their distinction remains causally active at every later position.

At the common exit s⁡(k)=32s(k)=32, no eligible suffix is exact in seven models and one is exact in three. The clean base run is not jointly readable there either (mean per-position agreement 38.1% over positions 9–32), so this contrast concerns readout time; it shows neither erased information nor a unique state code.

Localization and intervention controls.

Independent patch scans replace a width-one window of positions at loop ll. The maximal damage falls on position ll, the observed loop–position frontier, in 320/320 tested loop–seed cells. Prefix replacements that overwrite positions before an anchor are predominantly safe until the anchor passes this boundary: the first damaging anchor is l+1l+1 in 309/310 testable cases; the exception (seed 15, loop 31) is retained. Identical self-replacements do not change any predictions. Sources with the same symbolic state but a different history can still cause damage; they are not equivalent to self-replacement controls. Together, these results support a localized, causally sufficient computation under the specified intervention. They do not establish a pure or unique symbolic state code, nor use independent of machine context or execution phase.

The saved clean readouts in this position-8 audit include per-position accuracy, not clean whole-suffix exactness. In particular, a saved field for the base-target exactness of a patched run is not a clean baseline. We use explicit unpatched suffix metrics from the separate position-16 experiment when making clean-suffix comparisons.

A.5 Paired delayed and phase-crossing cohorts

The paired retention experiment freezes six models per supervision condition, seeds 9–14. It samples 256 different-state pairs and 256 same-state pairs per checkpoint, in sixteen batches of sixteen per pair kind. Pair identities are matched across conditions and seeds. The site stays at position c=16c=16; patch age a∈{0,1,2,4,8,16}a\in\{0,1,2,4,8,16\} means taking and inserting the source at loop 16+a16+a, rather than holding a loop-16 vector and inserting it later.

Shifted-frontier scoring uses s⁡(k)=k+as(k)=k+a. Fixed-exit scoring uses s⁡(k)=32s(k)=32 or 48. At fixed exit 32, increasing age reduces the remaining update count, and age 16 leaves no post-patch update. Shifted-frontier scoring fixes the update count to each target but still changes both source representation and base-run context. Neither age curve by itself identifies information decay.

The 242 different-state pairs with distinct complete suffix targets are the fixed denominator for source suffix exactness across all these schedules. Ordinary clean suffix exactness uses all 256 pairs. For a single target at distance d=1,2,4,8,16d=1,2,4,8,16, factual and source trajectories can have merged; single-target eligible counts are respectively 242, 207, 143, 90, and 35. Rates for an empty eligible set are undefined and stored as null, not zero.

The subsequent compatibility experiment reuses the pair identities and checkpoint configurations. It crosses source collection at cc or c+ac+a with base insertion at those same two loops, reading position c+dc+d after exactly dd further updates. The main descriptive slice is a=4,d=1a=4,d=1, with 242 eligible pairs. Its extent comparison instead inserts at loop p=c+ap=c+a and reads the unpatched position p+dp+d at loop p+dp+d. This latter slice has 121 eligible pairs, and the old site is five positions from the target while the current frontier is one position away. The two experiments are not interchangeable scoring slices. All 384 batches across twelve checkpoint conditions were validated for the compatibility cohort; the separate pilot is excluded.

A.6 Controls and statistical interpretation

True self-replacement copies the base run’s own vector at the same site and time, and must preserve predictions exactly. Same-symbolic-state sources come from another history and are a substantive intervention, not an identity control. A positive source score is interpreted alongside the clean base run’s agreement with its own target and with the source target. Chance coincidence with a source target is not causal transfer. A clean factual score is a reference level, not a formal upper bound on intervention performance.

Means first aggregate the specified pair/sample population within each model, then average models with equal weight. Model seeds are independent parameter initializations, whereas reused machine/pair samples are paired observations. We preserve per-seed outcomes rather than converting task pairs into a larger number of independent training runs. All intervals and differences in the main text are descriptive; no null-hypothesis significance claim is based on treating those repeated pairs as independent models.

Appendix B Additional results and their scope

B.1 Common-stream training controls

We compare five training conditions on the same three model seeds 9–11, checkpoint step 132,000, and held-out stream 20260923. The existing final-only and all-prefix checkpoints are re-evaluated; no baseline is retrained or selected by its score. Each model receives four batches of 128 examples at each horizon. The generator seed is 20260923+1009​H20260923+1009H, with identical generator configuration and batch layout across conditions. The H32 sweep covers r=1,…,96r=1,\ldots,96 and the H64 sweep r=1,…,192r=1,\ldots,192. Pairing rests on this deterministic generator specification; the original training-control evaluations did not save raw input hashes. Model seeds, rather than examples or loop counts, are the replication unit. The historical six-seed stream-20260909 results below remain a separate cohort and are not pooled into these comparisons.

One supervised position per example.

The new runs retain the original width 128, four attention heads, two shared layers, additive input injection, batch size 256, AdamW optimizer, and 35-stage, 132,000-update curriculum. Stage progression and the cosine learning-rate schedule are fixed, with no accuracy gate. Under sampled-prefix, the training budget is R=HR=H, as for the two serial baselines. Each example independently selects one position uniformly from 1,…,H1,\ldots,H and applies the original state and output cross-entropies there. If ℓb,k\ell_{b,k} denotes their weighted sum, the mean loss satisfies

𝔼⁡[1B​∑b=1Bℓb,Jb]=1B​H​∑b=1B∑k=1Hℓb,k,Jb∼U⁡{1,…,H}.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\ell_{b,J_{b}}\right]=\frac{1}{BH}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{k=1}^{H}\ell_{b,k},\qquad J_{b}\sim U\{1,\ldots,H\}.

Thus it is an unbiased estimator of the mean all-prefix loss. It changes position coverage while retaining one supervised position per example; it still requires intermediate trajectory labels and is not label-free. The saved control protocol, rather than the legacy configuration field supervision=final_only, identifies this objective.

Progressive and matched random exits.

We adapt the progressive loss of Bansal et al. (2022) to the same FSM Transformer. At horizon HH, set m=H+8m=H+8. Propose n∼U​{0,…,m−1}n\sim U\{0,\ldots,m-1\} and k|n∼U⁡{1,…,m−n}k\mid n\sim U\{1,\ldots,m-n\}; reject and redraw the complete pair when n+k<Hn+k<H. The accepted joint law is proportional to [m⁡(m−n)]−1[m(m-n)]^{-1} on H≤n+k≤mH\leq n+k\leq m, so neither accepted nn nor the exit is uniform. Both conditions optimize 12​Lm+12​Ln+k\tfrac{1}{2}L_{m}+\tfrac{1}{2}L_{n+k} using endpoint labels. The mm-loop branch has full gradients. For the random-exit branch, progressive runs nn loops without a gradient graph, detaches the hidden state, and differentiates through the remaining kk loops. Input embeddings are recomputed with gradients for injection into this continuation and absolute loop indices are preserved. The n=0n=0 case starts normally with gradients. matched random exit uses the same examples, draws, exits, and loss weights, but differentiates through all n+kn+k loops. At fixed weights and zero dropout, the two losses have equal values but different gradients. This is an FSM adaptation, not a reproduction of the original convolutional architecture, concatenated recall, or exit support; it is also distinct from the uniform Jitter-8 contract below.

Compute accounting.

Per update, both exit conditions execute F=m+n+kF=m+n+k forward blocks. The numbers of differentiable blocks are Bprog=m+kB_{\rm prog}=m+k and Bmatched=m+n+kB_{\rm matched}=m+n+k. Using a shape-aware matrix-multiply proxy with forward block cost b​N​L​(12​d2+2​N​d)bNL(12d^{2}+2Nd) and backward cost twice that amount (bb batch size, NN padded sequence length, LL shared layers), total work is 5.919×10165.919\times 10^{16} MACs for progressive and 7.438×10167.438\times 10^{16} for matched random exit per run. These exclude heads, embeddings, normalization, optimizer, and evaluation; they are proxies, not measured total FLOPs. Examples, updates, supervised exits, and forward work are matched, but backward work is not. The removed gradient path is the experimental intervention.

Attainment and retention.

The first four conditions reach 100% endpoint accuracy at r=32r=32 for all three seeds. sampled-prefix retains 99.80% endpoint accuracy and 96.03% whole-trajectory exactness at r=64r=64. The comparison supports an effect of supervision coverage without increasing the number of supervised positions per example. The small seed cohort and point estimates do not establish uniform or statistically demonstrated superiority over all-prefix. In contrast, progressive seeds 9 and 11 peak at only 59.38% and 52.73% endpoint accuracy: their low scores cannot be treated solely as forgetting. Seed 10 reaches 100% at r=40r=40 and 4848, then falls to 76.95% at r=64r=64 and 26.56% at r=96r=96. This fixed recipe provides no evidence of an additional progressive advantage, but does not establish a general ranking of progressive methods. The different outcomes under matched exits also show that supervision support alone does not determine retention; the gradient path matters in this comparison.

Length boundary.

No condition improves all H64 readouts. At r=64r=64, mean endpoint accuracy is 97.79%, 76.69%, 85.87%, 86.07%, and 33.92% for final-only, all-prefix, sampled-prefix, matched random exit, and progressive, respectively. At r=192r=192, the corresponding means are 17.12%, 72.72%, 60.61%, 53.71%, and 17.19%. These readout-dependent differences and the seed variation in Table A4 limit any inference from H32 retention to length generalization. This follow-up evaluates H64 only; it does not establish a new sampled length boundary over a range of longer horizons.

B.2 Historical six-seed endpoint accuracy

This subsection preserves the original seeds 9–14 on stream 20260909. Its results describe a different evaluation cohort from Tables A2–A4, even where model seeds overlap.

Table A6 gives the two over-budget slices that bracket the main comparison. All twelve models have endpoint joint accuracy 1.000 at the trained exit 32. The table makes clear that the six-seed mean at loop 64 does not imply identical behavior in every retained model.

B.3 Budget contracts and training support

A training contract assigns the number of repeated blocks to a sampled trace length. All examples in a training batch share that sampled horizon and loop count. Table A7 specifies the relevant contracts. Stochastic counts are drawn during training; their midpoint is used for a single-budget evaluation when no count is explicitly requested. Budget sweeps instead specify every evaluated loop count.

Matching recurrent work.

The Slack-4/Jitter-8 comparison fixes the architecture, final-only supervision, optimizer, curriculum, data seed, batch size 256, and 132,000 training steps. Each condition contains all six model seeds 9–14. Both have 𝔼⁡[R∣H]=H+4\mathbb{E}[R\mid H]=H+4. Replaying the training functions with their recorded random seeds gives the same sampled horizon sequence for both conditions. Define Cbatch=∑t=1132000RtC_{\mathrm{batch}}=\sum_{t=1}^{132000}R_{t}: this counts applications of the shared block to a complete batch, accumulated over the entire training run. It is not the loop count of one batch. The realized totals are 2,123,041 for Slack-4 and 2,121,730 for Jitter-8, a 0.06175% reduction for Jitter-8. The budget schedule is shared across model seeds. These counts measure recurrent block work, not complete training FLOPs: they are not weighted by actual padded sequence lengths and do not include embedding, readout, or optimizer costs. For comparison, Serial and Double accumulate 1,595,041 and 3,190,082 batch block applications under this curriculum; matching their optimizer steps does not match their recurrent work.

Endpoint retention and its tradeoffs.

Table A8 evaluates the frozen Slack-4/Jitter-8 models on the same length-32 stream, evaluation seed 20260909, with 512 examples per model. Every trained seed is included, including those that did not master the training length range. Jitter-8 has lower mean accuracy at the common exit 36 but retains much higher accuracy with further updates. Loops 48, 64, and 96 are outside both conditions’ H32 training support. The per-seed loop-64 slice in Table A9 shows that the retention advantage occurs in all six pairs, rather than arising from selection of successful Jitter-8 runs.

The wider valid-readout window does not imply uniformly better learning or length generalization. On the separate training-log evaluation stream (seed 20260902), five of six Slack-4 models and four of six Jitter-8 models reach .99 endpoint joint accuracy at every evaluated horizon 1–32. On the budget-sweep stream (seed 20260909), mean H64 endpoint joint accuracy at the common readout r=68r=68 is 74.32% for Slack-4 and 64.36% for Jitter-8. These length-OOD scores and the ID success counts use distinct evaluation streams; they are not pooled with the H32 retention measurements as one sample set.

The additional contracts provide different controls. The six audited Double models have τ⁡(k)=2​k−1\tau(k)=2k-1 and observed holds of two to five loops, but this comparison includes twice the recurrent work of Serial. Slack-8 does not match Jitter-8’s expected budget. Random-2x successes at H32 exits 32–64 are inside its training support and do not establish generalization to unseen loop counts; a deterministic mean-budget control for Random-2x is absent. These observations delimit what the budget experiments can attribute to the training exit distribution.

B.4 Whole-trajectory exactness and complementary contracts

Endpoint joint accuracy asks whether the final readout is correct. A stricter sample-level quantity asks whether every one of the H=32H=32 action positions has both its state and output correct. We call a sample satisfying this condition trajectory exact. This is not the same as the per-position marginal threshold used by the readability grids in Figure A2: one incorrect position makes a sample trajectory-inexact.

The same separation already appears at the trained exit: both Serial conditions have 100% endpoint accuracy at r=R=32r=R=32, whereas trajectory exactness is 0.10% for final-only and 100% for all-prefix. Thus the all-prefix result is not only a more reliable final readout; it preserves a substantially larger fraction of complete recurrent trajectories. For the matched-budget contracts, Jitter-8 similarly retains complete trajectories after the nominal support, while Slack-4 does not. These figures are descriptive paired-cohort means and do not establish that randomization is uniformly better inside the training support.

For context, two additional contracts delimit the interpretation of the retention comparison. Slack-8 is a deterministic extra-slack dose control: its H32 endpoint means are 100.00% at its trained exit R=40R=40, then 92.74%, 57.94%, and 44.21% at r=48,64,96r=48,64,96, respectively (six seeds, same stream and model recipe). It does not match Jitter-8’s expected budget. The audited Double cohort instead trains at R=2​HR=2H: on H32 it reaches 100% at its trained exit R=64R=64, but only 2.93% when forced to read at r=32r=32 (ten seeds). This positive control shows that long loops can be learned when they are the training contract; it is not a matched-compute estimate of the retention effect.

B.5 Length extrapolation

The sampled length boundary BfinalB_{\mathrm{final}} is the largest evaluated horizon whose last-position joint accuracy is at least .99, under the model’s own serial contract R=HR=H. It is a maximum over sampled horizons, not a proof of correctness at every intermediate or greater length. Table A11 reports the six paired values. The retention objective improves this metric in three seeds and reduces it in three, despite improving H32 answer retention. This does not establish that retention and length generalization are unrelated; it establishes that the observed retention gain does not provide a seed-wise guarantee of an improved sampled boundary.

B.6 Delayed swaps with their clean controls

The six paired final-only and all-prefix models of the original cohort receive interventions at position 16 of H32 inputs. The 256 different-state pairs are shared across models; 242 have distinguishable counterfactual targets. This population is fixed throughout, without selection on neural success.

At position 16 and loop 16, clean suffix exactness is 1.000 along the frontier in both conditions; source suffix exactness is 1.000 versus .939 (final-only versus all-prefix). At exit 32, clean exactness is .007 versus 1.000 and source exactness is .002 versus .722. Thus all-prefix supervision improves the common-exit readout of an early intervention, without improving frontier transport. Delaying both source collection and insertion by aa loops, and reading position kk at k+ak+a, holds the number of post-intervention updates fixed. Under all-prefix, clean suffix exactness stays at 1.000, but source exactness falls from .939 to .177, .102, and .000 at ages 1, 2, and 4. Even inserting the original loop-16 source at loop 20 fails: joint agreement with the position-17 counterfactual at loop 21 is 0%, compared with 94.63% when inserted at loop 16 and read at loop 17, while the late clean base run remains correct (Appendix B.7).

Table A12 places clean and source suffix exactness next to each other for the main delayed ages. Clean results score the unmodified base run’s own suffix over all 256 pairs; swap results score the source counterfactual on the fixed 242 eligible pairs. The two columns should not be subtracted as an effect estimate for a common target and denominator. Exit-48 values differ from exit-32 values by less than .036 across the reported condition/age entries. Unlike the shifted-frontier and exit-32 schedules, all-prefix clean suffix exactness at exit 48 is slightly below 1.000 (six-seed mean .9961; seed 11, .9766). This additional fixed exit does not remove the source-phase and base-phase changes inherent in delayed insertion.

B.7 Crossed times and replacement extent

Table A13 records the primary time-crossing slice from Appendix B.6. Each entry scores one target position and should not be compared as if it were complete-suffix exactness. At the early readout, clean factual correctness is 1.000 under both conditions; at the late readout it is .385 for final-only and 1.000 for all-prefix. The late final-only base run’s unmodified agreement with the source target is .167. These baselines prevent a raw late score from being mistaken for transferred information.

The extent comparison in Table A14 asks where an effective replacement can be made at the common loop 20. Its scored target, position 21, is never directly replaced. The downstream-only block includes position 20, which is the current frontier. Therefore its success supplies a localized positive reference, but neither it nor the larger block demonstrates that position 16’s old vector alone is sufficient. The old site’s extra distance to the target also prevents an equal-distance inference of state erasure.

B.8 Provenance of the principal quantities

The supplementary provenance index records each paired budget curve and original swap summary with its model seed, evaluation seed, checkpoint step, exact source path, SHA256 hash, and per-seed output. Twelve paired budget-sweep files and ten original swap files matched byte-for-byte between the local and remote evidence stores. The paired retention tables derive from the completed P1 result set, and the phase/extent tables from the validated compatibility follow-up. These later experiments use distinct pair populations and scoring slices from the original position-8 audit. They are not pooled into its numerator or denominator.

Low-dimensional alignment and bounded automaton extraction were explored in the wider project, but do not enter the present paper’s claims. The reported conclusions depend on the fixed-checkpoint behavioral evaluations, full-vector interventions, and paired training comparison described above.

Appendix C Local downstream recovery and source-phase controls

The phase-crossing experiment changes the base run’s entire execution phase. Here we keep the late background fixed and test whether changing one local downstream vector can restore the response to a fresh source. The protocol was fixed before inspecting this follow-up’s outputs; it did not retrospectively preregister the preceding experiments.

C.1 Population, interventions, and scoring

We evaluated all twelve frozen step-132,000 checkpoints: six final-only and six all-prefix models, with paired seeds 9–14. The experiment used H=32H=32 and the position-16 pair population, with 256 different-state pairs and 256 same-state/different-history controls per model. Source and base runs shared the machine, presentation, and future actions. The primary population was the fixed set of 242 different-state pairs whose symbolic state–output targets at position 17 differ. This selection used no neural predictions and was identical across arms and models. Same-state pairs had no distinguishable counterfactual target and were scored separately against their factual target.

Let hk,Srh_{k,S}^{r} and hk,Brh_{k,B}^{r} denote source and base vectors from unmodified runs. After loop 20, a single post-block, pre-final-normalization hook performed a 2×22\times 2 intervention:

i=1\displaystyle i=1 :h1620←h16,S16,\displaystyle:\quad h_{16}^{20}\leftarrow h_{16,S}^{16}, (7)
j=1\displaystyle j=1 :h1720←h17,B16.\displaystyle:\quad h_{17}^{20}\leftarrow h_{17,B}^{16}.

An index of zero left the corresponding late base vector unchanged. Thus (i,j)=(0,0)(i,j)=(0,0) was clean, (1,0)(1,0) inserted a fresh source, (0,1)(0,1) reset only the downstream position, and (1,1)(1,1) combined both changes. Both replacements in the combined arm were simultaneous. All other positions, including the table and remaining action positions, retained their loop-20 vectors. The reset therefore changed the scored position’s pre-update hidden state, using the base run’s own earlier vector; it did not insert a source position-17 vector or a symbolic answer. We ran one further shared-block update and read position 17 at loop 21.

The primary outcome was joint counterfactual accuracy: both predicted state and output at that position had to match the symbolic source continuation. It was neither factual accuracy nor suffix exactness. A fresh positive reference inserted h16,S16h_{16,S}^{16} at position 16 and loop 16 of the base run and read position 17 at loop 17. Secondary arms substituted the aged source h16,S20h_{16,S}^{20} at loop 20, with and without the same downstream reset.

C.2 Joint restoration recovers the fresh response

Table A15 and Figure A4 show that the combined intervention closely recovers the fresh reference under both supervision conditions. The all-prefix late clean arm has zero counterfactual accuracy because it correctly retains the distinct factual answer; its factual joint accuracy on these pairs is 100%. Neither a fresh source alone nor a downstream reset alone explains the combined result. For each model, we computed the paired interaction on the same eligible population,

I=A11−A10−A01+A00.I=A_{11}-A_{10}-A_{01}+A_{00}. (8)

The mean II was +70.32±22.39+70.32\pm 22.39 percentage points under final-only and +68.39±10.54+68.39\pm 10.54 under all-prefix, and was positive in all six models of each condition. These are descriptive within-model contrasts, with model seeds as the replication unit, rather than significance tests that pool reused task pairs as independent replications. Table A16 also exposes the substantial seed variation in final-only source-only performance.

Recovery extends beyond matching aggregate rates. Comparing the predicted state–output pair under the fresh reference and late combined intervention gives identical predictions for all 3,072 final-only model–pair evaluations (66 seeds, 22 pair kinds, 256256 pairs), and all but one of the 3,072 all-prefix evaluations. The exception is a different-state pair in seed 11 that succeeds under the fresh reference and fails after late restoration. This establishes agreement of discrete single-step behavior; it does not establish equality of the hidden states.

C.3 A readable aged source does not provide the same recovery

Source readability was measured at the actual source position used in the intervention, with the original state and output heads. Fresh sources were jointly correct on all different-state pairs in both conditions. Under all-prefix, aged sources were also 100% correct for both heads in every seed, over both the full 256-pair population and the 242 eligible pairs. Nevertheless, aged source plus reset reached only 26.31%, almost identical to reset alone at 26.17%. Its net gain was two successful model–pair evaluations across six sets of 242; the corresponding aged-source interaction was +0.14±0.34+0.14\pm 0.34 percentage points. The 26.31% level is therefore largely the reset baseline, not evidence of effective aged-source transport. Under final-only, the aged-source interaction was −0.14±0.34-0.14\pm 0.34 points, but aged source joint readability was only 39.88% on the eligible pairs. The cleaner evidence for readable yet non-interchangeable sources comes from all-prefix.

C.4 Controls, reproducibility, and interpretation

Same-state controls show that the downstream reset is a strong intervention: all-prefix factual accuracy falls from 100% to 25.13% with reset alone (Table A17). Fresh source plus reset restores 95.18%, matching the fresh reference and its roughly 4.8% substitution damage. For different-state eligible pairs, reset alone yields 26.17% source-correct, 20.94% factual-correct, and 52.89% matching neither target. Thus resetting does not itself provide a general accuracy repair, and complete-vector substitution cannot be interpreted as exchanging only a pure symbolic state.

True same-phase self-replacements were separately tested at position 16 with the fresh source, position 16 with the late source, late position 17, and both late positions. All preserved the corresponding clean predictions; saved pre-intervention invariants also passed. The evaluation reused stream 2026091001 in batches of 16, with batch streams formed by adding 10000019⋅kind index+1000003⋅batch index10000019\cdot\text{kind index}+1000003\cdot\text{batch index}. The separate 16-pair-per-kind execution pilot was excluded from all reported statistics. The experiment records contain the frozen protocol, checkpoint identities, pair identities, raw predicted and symbolic labels, and aggregate results. An independent scoring audit recomputed source rates and denominators from the recorded labels, without importing the aggregation implementation, and reproduced the reported results.

The positive result localizes a causal contribution of the downstream state: while the remaining network stays at its late phase, restoring one downstream vector together with a fresh source nearly reproduces the earlier single-step response. The aged-source comparison shows that downstream restoration alone does not make every readable source interchangeable. These conclusions are restricted to H=32H=32, insertion at position 16, reset of position 17, insertion at loop 20, and one subsequent update. Full-vector replacements can restore readiness, representation format, or other aspects of local compatibility; they do not identify a particular attention head, gate, or minimal state code. The experiment establishes neither information erasure nor necessity in unmodified execution, and does not demonstrate recovery of a whole suffix, length extrapolation, or the cause of natural endpoint deterioration from loop 32 to 33. That failure is localized by a separate experiment (Appendix E).

Appendix D Frontier freezing

D.1 Original cohort and protocol

The original freezing cohort uses the frozen checkpoints of Section 5 on a new evaluation stream (20260923), 512 inputs per model and horizon, with the same inputs for every arm of a given model. The schedule is fixed before scoring: models trained at R=HR=H use s⁡(k)=ks(k)=k. Frontier freezing captures position kk’s post-block hidden vector at loop s⁡(k)s(k) on the arm’s own ongoing trajectory and restores it after every later block. One loop later captures at s⁡(k)+1s(k)+1. Positions 1–8 freezes only those positions, so every later position must still compute. Readout cache runs the clean forward pass and delivers each position’s prediction saved at s⁡(k)s(k), without modifying any hidden state. No vector comes from a separate run, no label enters an intervention, and table and presentation tokens are never frozen. Frozen positions remain available to attention. All layers of a block still execute; freezing acts at recurrent block boundaries, not on individual layers or key–value caches. The protocol was written before the results were inspected but is exploratory, not an independent confirmation.

D.2 Additional observations and limits

Table A18 reports every evaluated model. Under frontier freezing, positions 1 and 2 remain correct and accuracy at each position’s scheduled capture loop falls from position 3 onward in all three groups. Capturing one loop later is not uniformly harmless. It lowers the endpoint to 74–77% in three of the twelve models at H=32H=32. On the separate H=64H=64 length evaluation at readout r=H=64r=H=64, it lowers the endpoint relative to clean in several final-only models (seed 12: 44.1% versus 99.2%; seed 14: 46.3% versus 95.7%). One-loop-later freezing is therefore a timing contrast, not a safe schedule. double models, whose observed clean frontier is τ⁡(k)=2​k−1\tau(k)=2k-1, collapse under both schedules; their clean endpoint at r=Hr=H is already low because they need about 2​H2H loops, so they are not interpreted. The readout cache preserves the captured predictions by construction and is correct on every original H32 example. It is the baseline any freezing schedule would have to beat; we propose no such schedule.

D.3 Freezing the new training controls

This follow-up evaluates all three sampled-prefix and all three matched random exit checkpoints from Appendix B.1, at step 132,000, without retraining. It was specified after inspecting their clean retention results and before inspecting their freeze results; it is exploratory. The fresh stream is 20260924, distinct from the 20260923 training-control evaluation. Each model uses 512 H32 examples in four batches of 128, evaluated for 64 loops. Saved input hashes match across all six models. Every model and all 512 examples are retained, without filtering on clean correctness. The two runtime pilots use a different stream and are excluded. progressive is outside this bounded follow-up: two models had not learned H32 and the successful model had a shifted clean frontier, requiring a separately specified schedule analysis.

Fixed schedules and eight arms.

The reference schedule s⁡(k)=ks(k)=k is fixed before evaluation and is not estimated from the new labels. The evaluator and its interventions are unchanged. Besides clean computation and readout caching, all-position freezing captures at sd​(k)=k+ds_{d}(k)=k+d for each d∈{0,1,2,4}d\in\{0,1,2,4\}; two prefix arms capture only positions 1–8 or 1–16 at kk. Each capture uses the arm’s own current vector after a whole block and restoration first affects the next loop. All remaining positions and presentation tokens stay live; attention can still use the held vectors. These interventions do not save FLOPs, use hidden states from another run, or establish layerwise or key–value cache freezing.

Clean eligibility.

All three sampled-prefix models have exact clean and cached H32 trajectories on this stream, including every diagonal readout at r=kr=k. For matched random exit, seed 11 also has exact diagonal reads; seed 10 has 99.80% minimum diagonal accuracy and 99.80% cached trajectory exactness. Seed 9 has 96.48% minimum diagonal accuracy, 94.92% cached trajectory exactness, and 99.80% clean endpoint accuracy. Thus the reference schedule s⁡(k)=ks(k)=k does not give perfectly correct clean readouts across this entire cohort; it is prescribed independently of the measured threshold-crossing loop τ⁡(k)\tau(k). The observed clean errors are reported as such; they are not evidence of a correct state failing under freezing. Even when the clean diagonal is exact, later vectors on an online-freeze trajectory may already be incorrect because earlier positions have been held. Clean readability at the reference schedule therefore does not imply that every vector actually captured under intervention is correct.

Capture-aligned and common readouts.

For a delayed arm, the endpoint has not yet been captured at r=32r=32. We therefore use r=32+dr=32+d for the endpoint comparison in the main figure and Table A20, with clean evaluated at the same loop. Common-loop scores at r=32,33,64r=32,33,64 are retained in full below. For example, sampled-prefix seed 10 scores 100% at r=32r=32 under delay 1 but only 82.81% when its endpoint is captured at r=33r=33; clean is 100% at both loops. Scoring only r=32r=32 would overstate the recovery. Scheduled whole-trajectory exactness reads each position at its own k+dk+d on the intervened trajectory. It differs from scoring every position simultaneously at a common loop. For prefix arms, the scheduled readout remains r=kr=k, including positions that are never frozen.

Results and limits.

Immediate freezing reduces mean endpoint accuracy to 4.10% for sampled-prefix and 6.25% for matched random exit, with zero whole-trajectory exactness in every model. Thus the failure to hold position states extends across these training objectives, including three models with fully correct clean scheduled reads. Delaying capture helps, but the required delay depends on the model and training condition. At delay 2, sampled-prefix reaches 99.80% mean endpoint accuracy and 99.54% scheduled trajectory exactness. matched random exit reaches only 87.24% endpoint accuracy at delay 2, and needs delay 4 to reach 99.80% endpoint accuracy and 99.74% scheduled trajectory exactness. All fixed delays and all seeds are reported; one loop is not a generally safe schedule. Prefix-only freezing also damages the never-frozen endpoint and suffix, so the collapse is not limited to scoring held positions. The two objectives differ in losses and training work, precluding a unique attribution of their delay difference to one training factor. These results concern holding a state on its own evolving trajectory; they do not demonstrate arbitrary vector interchangeability, convergence, or a particular microscopic circuit.

D.4 External maze network

We evaluated the released dt_net_recall_2d checkpoint (width 128, trained on 9×99\times 9 mazes for 30 iterations with the progressive loss of Bansal et al., 2022) without modification, on 32 pre-selected mazes per size for iterations 1–120. The recurrence was replayed by an external loop that reproduces the released forward pass exactly; a never-triggering hook reproduced the clean arm, and every arm matched clean before its first capture. Because there is no per-position frontier, a pixel’s capture time is its answer arrival: the last iteration at which its clean prediction changes (mean 6.2 at 9×99\times 9, 19.7 at 33×3333\times 33). Table A26 gives whole-maze solved counts.

The clean network solves every 9×99\times 9 maze from iteration 25 through 120, so it does not forget answers, yet freezing at answer arrival solves none. The limits are substantial. There is one checkpoint, no training seeds, and 32 mazes per size. Architecture, task, and objective differ from our models at once, so the check does not isolate any of them. The network’s output head is a 3×33\times 3 convolution stack, so holding a pixel’s state does not pin its prediction (2.9% of frozen pixels drift at capture +0+0, 0.3% at +4+4, 9×99\times 9); its frozen-readout quantities are not comparable with those of our per-position readout. The 33×3333\times 33 size lies outside the training distribution and its clean accuracy is still rising at iteration 120, so those comparisons are descriptive.

Appendix E Local recovery of the first natural failure

Protocol.

The evaluation uses the step-132000 final-only checkpoints (seeds 9–14, d=128d=128; stream 20260909) and three final-only models with d=512d=512 and four layers per block (seeds 9–11; stream 20260923), with H=32H=32 and 512 inputs per model. The primary cohort EE is fixed before any intervention: inputs whose endpoint is jointly correct at loop 32 and jointly wrong at loop 33. After loop 32, the listed positions are replaced by the model’s own vectors from an earlier loop of the same input, and loop 33 runs without further intervention. Every batch passed a whole-state replay check, a pre-patch invariance check, and a same-phase sham. The six all-prefix models have no member of EE, because their loop-33 endpoint accuracy is 100%; they have an empty rescue denominator, not a zero rescue rate.

Results and limits.

Pooled over the d=128d=128 models, the position-31, position-32, and combined resets recover 585, 143, and 771 of 771 members of EE. Loop-33 accuracy on all inputs is 89.5%, 35.2%, and 100%, against 74.9% clean. For d=512d=512 the counts are 41, 59, and 79 of 79, with all-input accuracy of 95.3%, 79.1%, and 100% against 94.9% clean. Single resets are not ranked: the position-31 reset leads in d=512d=512 seed 9, the position-32 reset in seeds 10 and 11, and a position-32 reset alone breaks between 130 and 350 correct inputs in every d=128d=128 model. The factorial interaction varies in sign across seeds, so we do not claim superadditivity.

The combined reset leaves positions 1–30 one loop ahead but otherwise approximately replays loop 32 at the endpoint, which was correct. Its success therefore localizes the first failure to the last two positions; it does not show that a restored state persists. Without a second intervention, d=128d=128 all-input accuracy at loop 34 is 63.7% after the combined reset versus 65.5% clean, whereas for d=512d=512 it is 93.4% versus 76.8%. We report the relapse as a d=128d=128 observation only. The experiment identifies joint sufficiency at one horizon and loop; it does not identify a circuit, show that either reset is necessary, or establish a repair method.
